subtopics.title: Article 3 and the procedure to rename a State
subtopics.summary: Article 3 empowers Parliament to reorganise States, including changing the name of a State. The Union Cabinet approved renaming Kerala as Keralam under this Article. A renaming Bill needs the President's prior recommendation and is passed by simple majority, without a constitutional amendment.
facts: Article 3 empowers Parliament to reorganise States.
Parliament can form a new State by separating territory from an existing State or by merging States or parts of States.
Parliament can increase or diminish the area of a State, alter its boundaries or change its name.
A Bill to rename a State can be introduced only with the prior recommendation of the President, which is mandatory.
The President acts on the advice of the Union Government.
The President refers the Bill to the concerned State Legislature.
The State Legislature can express its views within a specified period.
The opinion of the State Legislature is not binding.
The Bill is passed by simple majority in both Houses of Parliament.
No special majority or constitutional amendment is required.

subtopics.title: Articles 1, 2 and 4: Union, admission of States and status of such laws
subtopics.summary: Articles 1 to 4 sit under Part I, which deals with the Union and its Territory. Article 1 describes India as a Union of States, and Article 2 empowers Parliament to admit or establish new States. Article 4 makes clear that laws under Articles 2 and 3 are not amendments under Article 368, so they can pass by simple majority.
facts: Articles 1 to 4 fall under Part I, titled Union and its Territory.
India is called a Union even though its Constitution is federal in structure.
Article 1 describes India, that is Bharat, as a Union of States rather than a Federation of States.
Article 1 deals with two things: the name of the country and the type of polity.
Article 2 empowers Parliament to admit into the Union, or establish, new States on terms it thinks fit.
Admission under Article 2 refers to States already in existence; establishment refers to States not in existence before.
Article 4 declares that laws made under Articles 2 and 3 are not amendments under Article 368.
Such laws can therefore be passed by simple majority.
Names of States and Union Territories and their territorial extent are in the First Schedule.
At present, India has 28 States and 8 Union Territories.

subtopics.title: Integration of Princely States and the 1950 classification
subtopics.summary: At independence, India had British Provinces and Princely States. The Indian Independence Act (1947) gave Princely States three options, and 549 of 552 joined India. The Constitution of 1950 then classified the States and Territories into four parts.
facts: The Indian Independence Act (1947) created two independent dominions, India and Pakistan.
The Act gave Princely States three options: join India, join Pakistan or remain independent.
Of 552 Princely States within India's boundaries, 549 joined India.
The three that refused were Hyderabad, Junagarh and Kashmir.
Hyderabad was integrated by police action.
Junagarh was integrated by means of a referendum.
Kashmir was integrated by Instrument of Accession.
Part A: 9 erstwhile Governor's Provinces of British India.
Part B: 9 erstwhile Princely States with legislatures; Part C: erstwhile Chief Commissioner's Provinces and some Princely States.
Andaman and Nicobar Islands were kept as a solitary Part D territory.

subtopics.title: Linguistic reorganisation: commissions and the 1956 Act
subtopics.summary: The demand for linguistic States led to several commissions. The Dhar Commission favoured administrative convenience, the JVP Committee rejected language as a basis, and the Fazl Ali Commission broadly accepted language. The States Reorganisation Act (1956) then created 14 States and 6 Union Territories on 1 November 1956.
facts: The Dhar Commission (June 1948), chaired by SK Dhar, examined reorganisation on the linguistic factor.
The Dhar Commission recommended administrative convenience rather than the linguistic factor.
The JVP Committee (Dec 1948) consisted of Jawaharlal Nehru, Vallabhbhai Patel and Pattabhi Sitaramayya.
The JVP Committee formally rejected language as the basis for reorganisation of States.
The Fazl Ali Commission, a 3-member body, was appointed to re-examine the question in December 1953.
The Fazl Ali Commission broadly accepted language as the basis but rejected One Language - One State.
The Fazl Ali Commission suggested 16 States and 3 Centrally Administered Territories.
The States Reorganisation Act (1956) and a related amendment created 14 States and 6 Union Territories on 1 November 1956.
Andhra State (1953) was created by separating Telugu-speaking areas from Madras State.

quizzes.passage: The opening portion of the Constitution of India is concerned with the Union and its territory. It sets out the name of the country and the basic character of its government, even though the document gives the country a federal structure. The names of the States and Union Territories, along with the extent of their territory, are listed in a schedule to the Constitution, and the number of these units has changed over time. At the time of independence in 1947, the country was made up of British Provinces and Princely States. Legislation passed in 1947 had created two separate dominions, and the Princely States were given three choices: to join India, to join Pakistan, or to remain independent. Most of the Princely States joined India, although a few refused to do so at first. Those that stayed apart were later integrated by different means. The Constitution of 1950 then classified the States and territories into four groups. The same opening provisions allow Parliament to take up new States and changes to existing ones through laws it passes. Whether such laws must follow the procedure used for constitutional amendments is answered by the Constitution itself. Over the decades, the map of India has been redrawn several times, and each change has raised questions about the boundaries and identities of the regions concerned.

quizzes.passage: Demands for States organised on linguistic lines grew in several parts of the country after independence, and the government responded by setting up bodies to examine the question. Each of them examined the linguistic factor, but they did not reach the same conclusions. The creation of one State on a linguistic basis intensified demands from other regions, which pushed the government to take up the whole question again. Reorganisation was therefore examined more than once before a final framework was adopted. The change was made through a law passed by Parliament and a constitutional amendment passed in the same year. Together these measures shaped the map of India as it stood after that year. The original Constitution divided the States and Territories into four categories. A three-member commission was appointed to re-examine the whole question, and its suggestions included abolishing those categories. Under the Constitution, Parliament holds the power to reorganise States, which can involve forming a new State by separating territory, merging States, altering boundaries, or changing the name of a State. Later changes, such as the renaming of Orissa as Odisha, show that the same power has continued to be used. The bodies examined the linguistic question at different points in time.
